title: Triage Lighthouse Pattern and Runbook Deprecation Schedule
author: Asha Patel
body:
Summary
-------
This page defines the "Lighthouse" triage pattern for fast, deterministic incident routing and the governance cadence we use to deprecate, replace, or archive runbooks safely. The Lighthouse pattern focuses on a minimal, highly reliable signal path for first responders; the runbook deprecation schedule ensures playbooks remain accurate and unambiguous over time.

Scope
-----
- Applies to all public-facing and internal services that are covered by the incident-response program.
- Primary owners: SRE, Platform, and Serving Runtime teams.
- Excludes long-term strategic docs (design reviews, ADRs) which are governed by the architecture-doc lifecycle.

Why this exists
----------------
- Incidents often begin with noisy signals and inconsistent handoffs. The Lighthouse pattern reduces noise and forces deterministic routing to a small set of responders and runbook actions.
- Runbooks age quickly (config values, CLI tooling, playbook steps). A formal deprecation schedule reduces the risk of stale instructions during high-severity incidents.

Lighthouse Triage Pattern (high level)
-------------------------------------
Goal: get a single responder (the "Lighthouse") to a reproducible, verifiable triage state within 8 minutes of pager.

Principles:
- Minimal signal: use a single canonical metric (SLO breach / error rate / 5xx spike) + a corroborating log anchor or trace id.
- One point of accountability: Lighthouse is responsible for first 15 minutes of evidence collection and status.
- Fast fallbacks: if Lighthouse cannot validate within the timebox, escalation to the bridge owner occurs automatically.
- Automatable steps: runbook checks should be machine-verifiable (HTTP health endpoints, synthetic checks, KV cache stats).

Lighthouse flow (numbered run):
1. Alert fires -> Pager notifies L1 oncall (via PagerDuty).
2. L1 acknowledges within 90s and assumes Lighthouse role.
3. Lighthouse runs the "Lighthouse checklist" (below) and posts an initial status to the incident channel within 8 minutes.
4. If the checklist yields conclusive evidence (service down / config rollback required / capacity exhaustion), Lighthouse declares impact tier and requests bridge.
5. If inconclusive after 12 minutes, automated escalation promotes the bridge owner and notifies the product incident lead.
6. All actions and findings recorded in the incident timeline.

Lighthouse Checklist (essential checks)
--------------------------------------
- Check 1: Confirm alert anchor
  - Locate the canonical metric and a corroborating trace/log id (example: "req-id=abcd-1234 and service-load > 200 rps").
- Check 2: Scope impact (single-customer vs multi-tenant vs all customers).
- Check 3: Verify health endpoints: /healthz and /live. Expect 200 within 500ms.
- Check 4: Inspect recent deployments (last 30 minutes) via `gitlab deploys --since 30m --service <svc>`.
- Check 5: KV/cache metrics: cache hit ratio and eviction spikes (threshold: hit_ratio < 0.6 or eviction_rate > 100/s triggers cache investigation).
- Check 6: Check serving runtime resource saturation (GPU memory > 85% for > 60s, or CPU steal > 25%).
- Check 7: Run a quick synthetic request using the incident harness `infra/synthetics/run-on-demand --service <svc>` and capture latency + response signature.

Escalation ladder (fast path)
----------------------------
- Lighthouse (L1 responder) -> service steward (on-call engineer for owning service) within 12 minutes -> bridge owner (regional bridge operator) -> SRE incident lead -> Product incident lead.
- Automated escalations controlled by Alert Manager rules (escalate_after: 12m).

Communication templates (initial channel message)
------------------------------------------------
- Channel subject: [INC][P1] <service> - Observed error spike
- Message template:
  - "Observed: 5xx rate 3.2% (SLO: 0.5%), delta +2.9% in last 5m. Anchor: trace abc123. Tentative impact: multi-tenant. Lighthouse: @asha. Next step: run runtime/kv checks and request bridge if confirmed. ETA 10m."

Status page / Customer notice examples
------------------------------------
- Status page short (public):
  - "We are investigating elevated error rates for <service>. Some users may experience failures. We will provide updates within 30 minutes."
- Customer-facing email template (first comm):
  - Subject: Service interruption affecting <service> - investigating
  - Body: "Hello, we are investigating an issue causing intermittent failures for <service>. Our team has identified increased error rates and is actively working on containment. We expect an update within 30 minutes. If you need urgent assistance, reply to this message or contact your account team."

Runbook Deprecation Schedule (policy summary)
--------------------------------------------
Purpose: Provide a predictable, safe lifecycle for runbooks so oncall responders can trust playbook actions during incidents.

Key concepts:
- Active runbook: used in production incidents, must have owner, last-tested date, and automated verification hooks where possible.
- Stale runbook: older than 180 days without a test or owner update. Marked for review.
- Deprecated runbook: scheduled for archival 30 days after a deprecation notice unless revalidated.
- Archived runbook: moved to read-only archive with migration notes and the reason for retirement.

Runbook metadata requirements (every active runbook must include):
- owner: team and individual oncall alias
- last_tested: YYYY-MM-DD (date of last successful runbook smoke test)
- automated_checks: list of test jobs (CI job names or synthetic checks)
- minimum_slo_guard: the SLOs used to trigger the runbook (ex: 99.9p90 latency < 150ms)
- contact_escalation: explicit pager/alias and bridge owner

Deprecation cadence (process)
1. Detection: Repo scan job runs weekly to identify runbooks where last_tested > 180 days or missing metadata. A "stale-runbook" issue is created in the owning team's backlog.
2. Review window (30 days): Owner reviews and either updates last_tested, fixes metadata, or marks for deprecation.
3. Deprecation notice: If the owner does not revalidate, the doc is moved to the "deprecation" state and an automated notice is posted to the owning-team channel and the global runbook governance channel.
4. Grace period (30 days): During this period the runbook remains discoverable but is labeled DEPRECATED and shows the deprecation date.
5. Archive action: After the grace period, the runbook is moved to the archive folder and a change record is added linking to the replacement or rationale.

Runbook revalidation checklist (for owners)
-----------------------------------------
- Verify steps run end-to-end in the current environment (use test namespace).
- Update any CLI/command examples to match current tool versions.
- Confirm runbook automation jobs pass (CI: runbook-smoke-<svc>).
- Add or refresh synthetic checks that validate the primary symptoms the runbook addresses.
- Add a "game day" assignment: include the runbook in the next quarterly simulation if the runbook handles P1 or broad impact incidents.

Governance roles and responsibilities
------------------------------------
- Runbook Steward (team-level): maintain metadata and act on weekly stale-runbook issues.
- Runbook Czar (SRE): triage cross-team conflicts, final arbiter for forced deprecation when a service is retired.
- Automation Team: run the repo scan, maintain the smoke tests, and provide templates for runbook metadata.

Runbook metrics and observability
--------------------------------
Track these metrics in the Runbook Governance dashboard:
- Percent of active runbooks with last_tested < 90 days (target: 90%).
- Mean time between runbook edits (goal: balance stability vs freshness).
- Number of incidents where the runbook was used and the outcome (success / partial / failed).
- Runbook test failure rate (CI job failure rate).

Game day integration
--------------------
- Every quarterly game day includes a "Lighthouse drill" where oncall must complete the Lighthouse checklist against a simulated alert.
- Deprecated-runbook scenario: include at least one scenario per year that forces responders to discover a missing or deprecated runbook and to use the fallback procedures (service steward contact, quick rollback, or canary halt).

Templates and example automation (snippets)
-----------------------------------------
- Example runbook metadata header (YAML front matter):
  ---
  title: "cache-eviction-spike"
  owner: "platform-cache-team@redwood"
  last_tested: "2025-10-02"
  automated_checks: ["ci/runbook-smoke-cache", "synthetic/cache-hit-check"]
  minimum_slo_guard: "p99_latency < 300ms; cache_hit_ratio > 0.7"
  contact_escalation: "#platform-cache-oncall, pager:PD-service-cache"
  state: active
  ---

- CI job example (runbook smoke test):
  - name: runbook-smoke-cache
    script:
      - ./tools/runbook-smoke --run cache-eviction-spike --namespace test-infra

- Simple synthetic command for Lighthouse (example):
  infra/synthetics/run-on-demand --service serving-runtime --check "baseline-response" --tracing true

- Automation rule (Alertmanager pseudocode):
  - alert: High5xxRate
    expr: increase(http_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[5m]) / increase(http_requests_total[5m]) > 0.01
    for: 2m
    annotations:
      lighthouse_timeout: "12m"

Fallbacks and emergency rollback guidance
----------------------------------------
- If runbook steps require a deprecated CLI or API, use the emergency rollback play:
  1) Identify last-known-good deployment (tagged in CI).
  2) Execute `ci/rollback --service <svc> --to <tag>` and monitor the Lighthouse synthetic checks.
  3) If rollback fails, engage release engineering and escalate to SRE incident lead.

Retention, audit, and evidence requirements
------------------------------------------
- All incident actions that reference a runbook must include a runbook version or commit hash in the incident timeline.
- Deprecation actions and archive reasons must be logged in the governance repo with a link to the archived page.
- For any incident with regulatory impact, archived runbooks must be restored to an evidence folder and preserved with the incident artifacts.

Onboarding action items for new oncall members
---------------------------------------------
- Complete the Lighthouse primer (self-serve course) and pass the Lighthouse simulation (scoring >= 80%).
- Review the top 10 high-risk runbooks for their team and run the smoke tests locally.
- Shadow one live rotation and one game day exercise within first 30 days.

Appendix: Quick links and references
----------------------------------
- Runbook governance repo: gitlab.com/redwood/runbook-governance
- Runbook scanner: CI job `runbook-lifecycle-scan`
- Incident template (canonical): /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/incident-command-playbook-and-escalation-matrix-2024
